_note: Hand-checked summaries with links to the original reporting. Satellite comparisons are calculated live by the app. Counts in news reports use different methods from satellite detections.

india.why: Most fires are started by people, often while farming or clearing land, and hot, dry months provide the fuel. A Forest Survey of India study attributes over 95% of incidents to human activity.

events.title: Major fires in several states at once
events.summary: Odisha’s Similipal and Uttarakhand’s forests both burned that spring, after a very dry start to the year.

kerala.why: The hot months dry out undergrowth and bamboo, so fires spread easily. Officials and activists say most forest fires here are started by people, not lightning.

events.title: Drought year brings hundreds of fires
events.summary: After weak monsoons in 2016, the state’s forests minister reported about 440 fires and 2,100 hectares burned.

events.title: 150 hectares burn in Wayanad’s Banasura Hills
events.summary: Authorities filed a case of “unnatural fire”, with no arrests at the time of the report.

events.title: Fire on Kambamala hill, Wayanad
events.summary: About 10 acres reportedly burned. A fire this size barely changes a statewide total, which shows why this calendar suits seasons and not single fires.

punjab_haryana.why: Farmers burn leftover crop stubble to clear fields quickly between harvests: wheat stubble around April and May, and paddy stubble around October and November.

events.title: Crop fires feed Delhi’s smog
events.summary: Paddy burning continued while smog covered Delhi. Weather and Diwali fireworks also contributed.

events.title: Burning reportedly moves later in the day
events.summary: An ISRO-linked study reported that the peak moved from about 1:30 pm to about 5 pm, after the satellites pass. Punjab officials dispute this, but it means fewer detections may not equal less burning.

events.title: Official farm-fire counts fall sharply
events.summary: Reports described a marked decline in stubble-burning cases in both Punjab and Haryana.

northeast.why: Many fires come from jhum, or slash-and-burn farming, where hill plots are cleared before planting. In Mizoram, most reported forest fires happen in March.

events.title: Fires spread across south Mizoram
events.summary: Air Force helicopters joined the response. One serious fire can matter greatly to local people while barely changing the total for this wide region.

central.why: Spring fires burn through dry forest, and collectors of tendu leaves and mahua flowers sometimes use fire. Autumn fires are increasingly crop stubble, as more farmers grow paddy.

events.title: Madhya Pradesh tops the farm-fire count
events.summary: Reports placed Madhya Pradesh ahead of Punjab for the second year running. A ground report links it to farmers in Sheopur switching to paddy after rain damaged soybean and black gram.

odisha.why: A long dry season leaves forests full of dry leaves. Reported causes include burning leaf litter to collect mahua flowers and hunters setting fires, though the cause of a single fire is often unconfirmed.

events.title: Similipal burns for over 10 days
events.summary: Fires reportedly affected close to a third of the area of this tiger reserve, during a dry spell.

events.title: Odisha leads India in large fires
events.summary: Forest Survey of India data showed 642 large fire incidents in one week, after a dry spell since October.

uttarakhand.why: Before the monsoon, dry chir pine needles cover the forest floor and catch fire easily. Reported sparks include cigarette ends, campfires and burning debris.

events.title: Air Force helicopters fight the fires
events.summary: Disaster response teams and helicopters were sent in as fires spread across the hills, until rain helped bring them under control.

events.title: A very dry winter brings early fires
events.summary: Fires flared across Nainital, Almora and Tehri, and the Centre sent helicopters to help.

events.title: Five dead as fires spread
events.summary: Officials reported five deaths and about 1,300 hectares affected by 9 May.
